prompt: Shared serving reference. A support platform receives many requests about the same policy document. The document defines a prefix cache as a store of already-computed key-value attention states for an identical beginning of a request. The cache is useful only after a request has produced reusable blocks, and a later request begins with the same token sequence. A cache lookup must compare token blocks, locate an existing entry, attach its key-value states to the new request, and continue prefill only from the first unmatched block. The cache does not skip decoding: every newly generated token still needs a forward pass. The service uses fixed-size cache blocks, so a shared prefix shorter than one block or ending just before a block boundary may save little work. A cache can also add hash computation, metadata lookup, eviction bookkeeping, and memory pressure. A good evaluation therefore compares cache-off and cache-on under the same model, dtype, prompt distribution, generation length, concurrency, warmup, and request order. It records direct cache evidence from backend metrics or logs, not merely a change in latency. It also reports TTFT because prefix reuse primarily avoids prefill work, TPOT because decode remains largely unchanged, end-to-end latency, successful requests, and output throughput. If the prefix is short, lookup cost can exceed saved prefill even when the hit rate is high. If the prefix is long and many requests reuse it, the saved prefill can dominate. A cache entry must be isolated by model, tokenizer, and compatible request state. It may be evicted when the KV capacity is needed for active decoding. The service keeps an evidence record for every run: model revision, tokenizer, dtype, cache block size, cache capacity, execution order, request count, warmup count, generation length, successful and failed request counts, and the exact source of any cache metric. A fair cache-off baseline still runs the same prompt sequence and performs the same client-side serialization; it changes only the backend prefix-cache switch. The warmup requests are deliberately identical in structure to later measured requests so that the candidate has a real opportunity to create reusable blocks before measurement. The baseline has no reusable blocks even when requests repeat. When two service launches are compared, their absolute latency can drift because of GPU clocks, allocator state, or background activity. Reversing the launch order in a later run therefore checks whether the sign of the cache effect survives that drift. A deployment decision needs both the mechanism observation and the endpoint metrics; neither one substitutes for the other. The experiment below uses a long common reference followed by a different question for each request. Do not infer a cache hit from TTFT alone; use the backend cache metric or server log as the causal observation. Question 01: summarize why a prefix cache mainly changes prefill rather than decode.
